Full per-unit lessons for all eight units are below, followed by exam orientation, worked free-response questions, and a 50-question practice exam. For interactive visual intuition on any concept, the Calculus subject carries matching explorers you can drag and explore.
AP Calculus AB covers single-variable differential and integral calculus across eight units, assessed by a multiple-choice and free-response exam.

• Section I: Multiple Choice (50% of total score, 45 questions, 105 min):
    • Part A (60 min, 30 questions, NO calculator): Average 2 minutes per question. Prioritize standard derivatives, integrals, and graphical interpretations.
    • Part B (45 min, 15 questions, Graphing calculator required): Average 3 minutes per question. Use your calculator efficiently for graphing intersections, numerical derivatives (nDeriv), and numerical definite integrals (fnInt).
  • Section II: Free Response (50% of total score, 6 questions, 90 min):
    • Part A (30 min, 2 questions, Graphing calculator required): Typically involves rate in/rate out accumulation or area/volume/motion.
    • Part B (60 min, 4 questions, NO calculator): Graph of derivative analysis, separable differential equations, Riemann sum approximations with error, and particle motion. You may continue to write on Part A during this time, but without a calculator.
  • Composite Score Threshold: A composite score of roughly 68–72% yields a 5, and ~55–60% yields a 4. Maximizing points on setup and theorem statements across every FRQ is the single most effective strategy for reaching a 5.

label.en: 💡 The 4 Big Ideas of AP Calculus AB

body.en:
• Big Idea 1: Change (CHA): Calculus models how quantities change continuously. Derivatives express instantaneous rates of change, while differential equations relate rates to current states.
  • Big Idea 2: Limits (LIM): Limits provide the mathematical foundation for both the derivative (limit of difference quotients) and the definite integral (limit of Riemann sums). Continuity and asymptotic behavior depend entirely on limits.
  • Big Idea 3: Analysis of Functions (FUN): Calculus connects a function \( f \) with its first derivative \( f' \) (growth, extrema) and second derivative \( f'' \) (concavity, inflection points) both algebraically and graphically.
  • Big Idea 4: Integration & Accumulation (INT): The definite integral calculates the accumulated net change of a rate over time. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) unifies differentiation and integration as inverse processes.

label.en: ⚠️ Authentic AP Calculus AB Exam Traps & Pitfalls

body.en:
• Equating directly to indeterminate forms: Writing \(\lim = \frac{0}{0}\) or \(\lim = \frac{\infty}{\infty}\) is penalized by AP readers. Always evaluate numerator and denominator limits separately before applying L'Hôpital's Rule.
  • Omitting hypotheses in theorem justifications: Citing MVT, IVT, or EVT without stating that the function is continuous on \([a, b]\) (and differentiable on \((a, b)\) for MVT) forfeits justification points.
  • Rounding prematurely: Intermediate rounding in calculator-active problems causes final discrepancies. Always keep full precision in your graphing calculator and round or truncate only the final answer to 3 decimal places.
  • Confusing absolute extrema with local extrema: The First Derivative Test proves local extrema only. To find absolute extrema on a closed interval, you must use the Candidates Test evaluating all interior critical points and endpoints.

question.en: On the AP Calculus AB exam, Section I (Multiple Choice) consists of 45 questions worth 1 point each, and Section II (Free Response) consists of 6 questions worth 9 points each (54 points). Each section accounts for 50% of the composite score. If the composite score is scaled out of 108 total points, what is the weighting multiplier applied to the raw Section I MCQ score and to the raw Section II FRQ score?

solution.en:
Step 1: Determine total points allocated to each section: \[ \text{Points per section} = \frac{108}{2} = 54\text{ composite points}. \]

Step 2: Find the MCQ conversion factor: \[ \text{MCQ multiplier} = \frac{54\text{ composite points}}{45\text{ raw points}} = 1.20. \]

Step 3: Find the FRQ conversion factor: \[ \text{FRQ multiplier} = \frac{54\text{ composite points}}{54\text{ raw points}} = 1.00. \]

Therefore, each multiple-choice question contributes \(1.2\) composite points, while each free-response point contributes \(1.0\) composite point to the scaled 108-point total.

question.en: A student correctly answers 32 out of 45 questions on Section I (MCQ) and earns 34 out of 54 points on Section II (FRQ). Using the standard College Board composite scaling (MCQ raw \(\times 1.2\) + FRQ raw \(\times 1.0\)), calculate the student's composite score and determine if they exceed the typical cutoff of 68 points needed for a top score of 5.

solution.en:
Step 1: Calculate weighted Section I score: \[ 32 \times 1.2 = 38.4\text{ points}. \]

Step 2: Calculate weighted Section II score: \[ 34 \times 1.0 = 34.0\text{ points}. \]

Step 3: Sum composite points: \[ \text{Composite score} = 38.4 + 34.0 = 72.4 \approx 72\text{ points}. \]

Because \(72.4 > 68\), this composite score comfortably earns an AP score of 5.
